newsitem.title: USA: Germans must embrace change-Commerzbank CEO.
newsitem.headline: Germans must embrace change-Commerzbank CEO.

text.p: Germans must become more open to change if their economy is to hold its own in an increasingly competitive world and cut its high unemployment, Commerzbank chief executive Martin Kohlhaussen said on Sunday.
"It is the great weakness of the German economy that, in political circles and in society generally, structural change is considered a threat," Kohlhaussen said.
"What we need is a positive attitude to change and adjustment if we want to be successful in a globalised economy and intend to achieve an adequate level of employment again."
Kohlhaussen called for increased deregulation in the German market, adding that this would help to draw investment into the country.

He welcomed such changes as the recent legislation to lengthen the country's highly restricted shop opening hours, but said such decisions took too long and were thus only implemented after great delays.
"It is high time that deregulation measures were implemented and greater flexibility was introduced in the business sector, as has long been promised," he said.

"If it takes Germany 10 years to extend shop opening times by 1-1/2 hours a day, we cannot expect foreign investors to take the country seriously when they are choosing a business location," he added.

Issues such as workers' worries that they would be forced to work longer hours if stores were open longer -- and even consumer concern that plans for variable opening hours would lead to uncertainty about which store was open when -- played a part in delaying the decision to extend shop hours.
Even the stores themselves resisted change for years, arguing that longer hours simply meant higher costs, with no guarantee of increased turnover.

But Kohlhaussen said there were signs that Germany was beginning to show a greater awareness of the need for change to keep up with rival economies, adding that this could give grounds for optimism that more flexibility was on the way.
"I think there will be more to come," he said.
